prompt.context: Our client is an organization trying to incentivize pharma and biotech firms to develop treatments and vaccines for diseases that are prevalent in developing countries. Their challenge is to identify where to focus as there are many possible diseases.
prompt.question: Which diseases represent the best opportunity for our client to focus on?

clarifying_info.a: DALY stands for Disability-Adjusted Life Year and is a measure of how much impact a disease has on peoples' productivity. Diseases which cause people to die young or which cause disability starting in childhood have the highest DALY scores.

clarifying_info.q: What does Pipeline mean in the exhibit?
clarifying_info.a: Pipeline indicates the number of drugs that are currently under development.
All these data are made up, as are some of the disease names.
Etiology means the causes of the disease.
Antigen is a general term that can refer to anything which provokes an immune response, whether bacteria, virus, etc.

clarifying_info.q: Do the bars in the etiology chart sum to 100%?
clarifying_info.a: No. Some cases are caused by antigens that have not yet been identified, so the bars do not sum to 100%.

clarifying_info.q: How recent are the etiology data and how large are the samples?
clarifying_info.a: Data are from last year. Sample sizes are n=1500 for the local population (children under 18) and n=256 for the military (soldiers of all ages).

clarifying_info.q: How should I read the prescribing chart (Exhibit 3)?
clarifying_info.a: The chart shows physicians in each market arranged by their prescribing level of the product horizontally in descending order — the highest prescriber is on the left. The height of the line represents the cumulative total of all units they have prescribed.

exhibits.title: Disease Burden vs. Pipeline for Developing-Country Diseases
exhibits.shows: A scatter plot or bubble chart with diseases plotted by DALY score (disease burden) on one axis and number of drugs currently in the development pipeline on the other axis. Diseases shown include HIV, Hepatitis (Hep), TB, Malaria, and Diarrheal Disease, among others.
exhibits.data: HIV and Hep have the highest DALY scores and also the most pipeline drugs. TB, Malaria, and Diarrheal Disease have the next-highest disease burden. Diarrheal Disease has the fewest products in the pipeline among the mid-burden diseases.

exhibits.title: Etiology of Diarrheal Disease — Incidence by Antigen
exhibits.shows: A bar chart showing the percentage of diarrheal disease cases (incidence) attributable to each identified antigen, with separate bars for the local population and the military. The Y-axis is incidence (percent of cases). Multiple antigens (Antigen A, B, C, etc.) are shown.
exhibits.data: 5% of cases are caused by Antigen A (example bar). No single antigen dominates; many antigens each account for a small share. Bars do not sum to 100% because some cases come from unidentified antigens. Local population sample n=1500 (children under 18); military sample n=256 (soldiers of all ages).

exhibits.title: Prescribing Distribution by Physician — Market 1 vs. Market 2
exhibits.shows: A cumulative prescribing chart with physicians on the X-axis arranged from highest to lowest prescriber, and cumulative units prescribed on the Y-axis, with two lines representing Market 1 and Market 2.
exhibits.data: In Market 1, approximately 80% of units are prescribed by roughly the top one-third of physicians. In Market 2, approximately 80% of units are prescribed by roughly the top 60% of physicians. Market 1 is more concentrated than Market 2.

framework: Identify disease burden vs. pipeline gap: plot diseases by DALY (impact) against existing pipeline to find underserved high-burden diseases
Understand disease complexity: assess whether a single treatment or vaccine is feasible given the range of causative agents
Identify customer segments: map who would purchase a new treatment or vaccine (governments, international orgs, military, tourists)
Assess commercial risks per customer: pricing power, negotiating leverage, volume commitment, pre-commitment mechanisms
Analyze market structure: evaluate prescribing concentration to prioritize geographic markets for launch

questions.prompt: Looking at Exhibit 1, which diseases represent the best opportunity for the client to focus on?
questions.guidance: Strong answer identifies that high DALY + low pipeline = best opportunity. HIV and Hep have high burden but crowded pipelines, so marginal impact of incentivizing more development is low. TB, Malaria, and Diarrheal Disease have the next-highest burden. Among these, Diarrheal Disease has the fewest pipeline products, making it the most underserved and the clearest focus area.

questions.prompt: The client has decided to focus on diarrheal disease. Looking at Exhibit 2, what does this tell us about diarrheal disease?
questions.guidance: Strong answer notes that diarrheal disease is not caused by a single primary antigen but by many different ones — analogous to the flu with multiple strains. This makes developing a universal treatment or vaccine difficult because it must be effective across many antigens, not just one. The bars not summing to 100% makes the problem even harder. This complexity explains why so few treatments currently exist.

questions.prompt: Who would be the main customers if a treatment or vaccine for diarrheal disease were developed?
questions.guidance: Candidates should brainstorm beyond the obvious. Key segments: (1) Governments of affected developing countries — large-volume buyers; (2) International nonprofits and organizations such as the WHO/UN — procurement agents for developing-country programs; (3) Military — soldiers deployed to endemic regions; (4) Foreign tourists traveling to endemic regions. Interviewer should prompt 'who else?' until military and tourists are identified.

questions.prompt: What are the issues or risks the drug maker would face with each customer segment?
questions.guidance: Governments and military buy in large volumes but have significant negotiating power. A single decision by the military not to buy could render the whole project unprofitable. Risk mitigation: pre-commitment contracts. Tourists are a fragmented, price-insensitive segment but smaller volume. International orgs may have budget constraints and slow procurement cycles.

questions.prompt: Looking at Exhibit 3, what does the prescribing data show and which market seems like a better target?
questions.guidance: Market 1 is more consolidated: ~80% of units come from roughly the top one-third of physicians. Market 2 requires the top ~60% of physicians to account for 80% of units. A concentrated prescriber base means a smaller sales force can cover most of the market opportunity — Market 1 is the better initial target because fewer physicians need to be educated and reached to achieve high penetration.

math.setup: Read cumulative prescribing curves: at the 80th percentile of cumulative units, find the corresponding share of physicians on the X-axis for each market.
steps: Market 1: 80% of cumulative units are prescribed by approximately the top 33% (one-third) of physicians
Market 2: 80% of cumulative units are prescribed by approximately the top 60% of physicians
Market 1 is roughly 2x more concentrated than Market 2
math.answer: Market 1 is the better target due to higher prescriber concentration — fewer physicians to reach for the same revenue impact.

brainstorming.prompt: Who would be the main customers if a treatment or vaccine for diarrheal disease were developed?

categories.name: Public sector / governments
ideas: Governments of developing countries where diarrheal disease is endemic

categories.name: International organizations
ideas: Other UN agencies and global health funds

categories.name: Military
ideas: Armed forces of countries deploying soldiers to endemic regions
US military, NATO forces on overseas deployments

categories.name: Travelers and tourists
ideas: Foreign tourists traveling to endemic regions
Employers sending workers to endemic areas

recommendation: Focus incentive efforts on diarrheal disease, which has a high DALY burden and the lowest existing pipeline of the mid-burden diseases
The complexity of the disease (multiple causative antigens) is addressable but requires broad-spectrum treatment or vaccine development, and explains the current gap
Target Market 1 for commercial launch given its concentrated prescriber base, enabling efficient sales force deployment
risks: Multi-antigen complexity may make vaccine development technically infeasible or very expensive
Large customers (governments, military) have significant negotiating power and could suppress margins or withdraw, jeopardizing viability
Cases from unidentified antigens (the bars not summing to 100%) mean the disease burden is even harder to address fully
next_steps: Establish pre-commitment procurement contracts with governments and military buyers before investing heavily in development
Conduct scientific feasibility study on broad-spectrum vaccine or treatment options
Quantify the tourist and military market sizes to validate commercial viability alongside the public-sector opportunity
